questions.stem: The review compares change management to 'air traffic control.' What is the purpose of this process?

choices.text: To eliminate the need for documentation
To prevent changes from crashing into each other and causing downtime
To speed up changes by skipping approvals
To assign IP addresses to new devices

questions.explanation: Change management coordinates modifications so they don't collide and cause downtime or accidents - like air traffic control for the organization.
questions.trap: The goal is controlled coordination, not skipping approvals or speeding changes through unchecked.

questions.stem: In change management, what is the difference between 'scope' and 'impact'?

choices.text: Scope is the cost; impact is the calendar date
Scope is the rollback plan; impact is the backup plan
Scope is how far the change reaches; impact is the consequence of making it
Scope and impact are two words for the same thing

questions.explanation: Scope is how far the change reaches (one laptop vs the whole data center); impact is the consequence (e.g. taking the internet offline to reboot a firewall).
questions.trap: Scope and impact are distinct: reach versus consequence. They are not interchangeable.

questions.stem: Using the SNE mnemonic for change types, which describes a low-risk, pre-approved change like replacing a broken mouse?

choices.text: Standard change
Normal change
Emergency change
Scheduled change

questions.explanation: A standard change is low risk and pre-approved, like swapping a broken mouse - no full approval cycle needed.
questions.trap: A normal change is medium risk and requires the full approval process; the mouse swap is the pre-approved standard type.

questions.stem: A zero-day vulnerability must be patched immediately to stop a critical threat. Which change type is this?

choices.text: Standard change
Normal change
Routine change
Emergency change

questions.explanation: An emergency change is high risk and happens immediately to stop a critical threat such as a zero-day vulnerability.
questions.trap: A normal change goes through the full approval cycle first; an active critical threat can't wait, making it an emergency change.

questions.stem: During the holiday shopping season, a retailer forbids all changes to its systems. What is this called?

choices.text: A maintenance window
A change freeze
A rollback plan
A sandbox

questions.explanation: A change freeze blocks all changes during critical business periods like the holiday shopping season.
questions.trap: A maintenance window is the opposite - a pre-approved time when changes ARE allowed, usually during low usage.

questions.stem: When is a maintenance window typically scheduled?

choices.text: During peak business hours for maximum staff coverage
Only during a declared change freeze
A pre-approved low-usage time, such as Sunday at 2 a.m.
Immediately whenever a technician feels like it

questions.explanation: Changes usually happen during a maintenance window - a pre-approved time when usage is low, like Sunday at 2 a.m.
questions.trap: You schedule changes when usage is LOW, not during peak hours, to minimize disruption.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a rollback plan and a backup plan in change management?

choices.text: A rollback plan returns the system to its original configuration if the change fails; a backup plan is your plan B for the implementation itself
A rollback plan is your plan B for implementation; a backup plan restores the original config
They are the same thing with different names
A rollback plan only applies to hardware; a backup plan only applies to software

questions.explanation: A rollback plan reverts the system to its original config when a change fails. A backup plan is your plan B for the implementation (e.g. a flash drive ready in case the internet drops mid-patch).
questions.trap: Don't swap them: rollback = undo the change; backup plan = alternative way to carry out the implementation.

questions.stem: Which body acts as 'mission control,' reviewing the risk of a change and granting permission to proceed?

choices.text: The sandbox
The change control board (CCB)
The CMDB
The SLA committee

questions.explanation: The change control board (CCB) reviews the risk and grants permission to launch a change.
questions.trap: The sandbox is where you TEST the change; the CCB is who APPROVES it.

questions.stem: Before touching the live network, where should a change be tested safely?

choices.text: Directly on production during peak hours
On the CEO's workstation
In a sandbox (a self-contained test environment)
Only in the rollback plan document

questions.explanation: A sandbox is a self-contained 'flight simulator' where you can crash safely without affecting the live network.
questions.trap: Testing on production or a real user's machine defeats the purpose; the sandbox isolates the risk.

questions.stem: A change has been deployed and appears to work. According to the review, the change isn't truly complete until what happens?

choices.text: The ticket is deleted
The next maintenance window opens
A new purchase order is issued
End users confirm everything works (end-user acceptance)

questions.explanation: The mission isn't over until end-user acceptance - the people who actually use the system confirm it works as expected.
questions.trap: Deleting the ticket prematurely skips verification; you need end-user acceptance to close out a change.
